Q: Unable to inspect Android device via Chrome://inspect A:

What works for me immediately is to ensure that you have adb and Android platform tools installed.

Phone: Enable the Developer Mode and USB Debugging

PC / Mac / Linux

  • Type in adb shell in Command Prompt / Terminal (Accept the debugging prompt on the phone and keep the terminal running)

  • Go back to Chrome and type in chrome://inspect/#devices

Almost every time, on the Android, the running browsers apps and webpages should be visible to inspect.

Hope this helps!

Q: Is it possible to execute package wrapped into archive as module A:

It seems you ought to package up your module as a module inside the zip file. Which is not something the built-in zipapp packager makes particularly easy. Which is why I came up with this script to generate the .pyz file instead:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import argparse
import zipfile
import pathlib
import os


def parse_args():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()

    parser.add_argument(
        'source',
        type=pathlib.Path)
    parser.add_argument(
        '--output', '-o',
        type=pathlib.Path,
        required=True)

    return parser.parse_args()


args = parse_args()

with args.output.open('wb') as outf:
    outf.write(b'#!/usr/bin/env python3\n')

    modname = args.source.name
    files_to_add = args.source.rglob('*')

    with zipfile.ZipFile(outf, 'w') as outz:
        outz.mkdir(args.source.name)
        for child in files_to_add:
            if child.suffix == '.pyc' or child.name == '__pycache__':
                continue
            arcname = child.relative_to(args.source.parent)
            outz.write(child, arcname.as_posix())

        outz.writestr('__main__.py', (
            f'__import__("runpy").run_module('
                f'{modname!a}, '
                f'run_name="__main__")'
            ).encode('utf-8'))


    os.chmod(outf.fileno(), 0o755)

In other words, instead of creating this structure inside your .pyz file:

.pyz
├── __main__.py (your own)
└── ⟨other module files⟩

you get this:

.pyz
├── ⟨your module⟩
│   ├── __main__.py (your own)
│   └── ⟨other module files⟩
└── __main__.py (forwards to ⟨your module⟩.__main__)

Q: How do I check whether a file exists without exceptions? A:

Code:

import os
check_if_path_exists=lambda path: os.path.exists(path)

or:

import os
def check_if_path_exists(path):
    return os.path.exists(path)

This code checks whether the file or path specified by the argument path exists using the os.path.exists() function. It checks if the path exists and returns True if it exists and False if it doesn't exist. Example:

check_if_path_exists("..") # True
check_if_file_exists("bjkjkjnkjnkjnkjnkjnkjn") # Most likely False

NOTES:

  • check_if_path_exists can be replaced with from os.path import exists or from os.path import exists as check_if_path_exists.

  • If you want to check if it is a file, you would want to substitute it with os.path.isfile. There's also:

    • isdir (folders),
    • isfifo (usually nix-only - FIFOs/named pipes),
    • islink (is symlink - always returns False on older Windows versions with no symlink support),
    • ismount (is a directory where other device is mounted, partial support on Windows),
    • isjunction (Windows-only - is directory junction, always returns False on NIX),
    • and issock (nix-only - is Unix domain socket. On Windows, always returns False)

    as these also check if they exist.

Q: Sanitizing JSON with @RequestBody A:

You can write a custom sanitizer using @Around an Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP) advice used to intercept and execute custom logic both before and after a target method runs.
